# Green Party 2024 Manifesto Summary

## Overview

The Green Party's 2024 manifesto addresses the cost of living crisis, climate emergency, and public service decline. It proposes significant public investment funded through wealth taxation and borrowing.

## Health and Social Care

The manifesto proposes £28bn additional annual NHS spending by 2030, plus £20bn capital investment over five years. Key commitments include reducing waiting lists, guaranteeing GP access, ensuring NHS dentist availability for all, boosting staff pay, and restoring public health budgets. The party opposes NHS privatisation and supports the NHS Reinstatement Bill.

For social care, the manifesto proposes £20bn annual investment, free personal care, improved pay and career structures for carers, and increased disability benefits by 5%.

## Housing

The manifesto targets 150,000 new social homes annually, ending right-to-buy, empowering councils to introduce rent controls, and ending no-fault evictions. A £29bn five-year programme would retrofit homes for energy efficiency, with additional funding for heating systems and climate adaptation.

## Energy and Environment

The party proposes no new oil and gas licences, ending fossil fuel subsidies, and targeting 70% wind-generated electricity by 2030. Community ownership of energy infrastructure would be encouraged. Water companies would return to public ownership.

Environmental commitments include a Rights of Nature Act, protecting 30% of land and seas by 2030, and £1.5bn additional DEFRA funding.

## Economy and Taxation

The manifesto proposes £40bn average annual green investment, including £50bn each for electricity infrastructure and building retrofits, £30bn for rail electrification, and bringing railways, water companies, and major energy retailers into public ownership.

Revenue would come from a wealth tax (1% on assets over £10m, 2% over £1bn), aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates, reforming inheritance tax, and a carbon tax starting at £120 per tonne. The party estimates raising £50-70bn annually from tax reforms.

## Welfare and Work

Proposals include increasing Universal Credit by £40 weekly, abolishing the two-child benefit cap, ending the five-week benefit wait, and increasing carer's allowance by 10%. The party supports a £15 minimum wage, maximum 10:1 pay ratios, repealing anti-union legislation, and moving toward a four-day working week.

## Education

The manifesto proposes £8bn additional school funding, £2.5bn annually for building repairs, £5bn for special needs provision, scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, and free school meals for all children.

## Transport

Commitments include £10bn annual public transport subsidies, bringing railways into public ownership, £2.5bn annually for cycling and walking infrastructure, free bus travel for under-18s, and ending new petrol/diesel vehicle sales by 2027.

## Democracy and Rights

The party supports proportional representation, votes at 16, replacing the House of Lords with an elected chamber, repealing the Elections Act 2022, and defending the Human Rights Act.

## Immigration

The manifesto proposes ending the hostile environment policy, creating safe asylum routes, allowing asylum seekers to work during applications, and removing minimum income requirements for spousal visas.

## International Affairs

Key positions include supporting an immediate bilateral ceasefire in Gaza, recognising Palestine, ending UK arms exports to Israel, rejoining the EU, increasing overseas aid to 1% of GNI, and signing the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons while cancelling Trident.

## Funding

The manifesto projects a deficit of £85.3bn in year one, funded by borrowing, decreasing as tax revenues increase. By 2030, projected revenue spending reaches £161.6bn with capital spending of £90.3bn, offset by estimated tax revenues of £172.4bn.
